newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Western envoy in talks to halt new Albania crisis.
newsitem.headline: Western envoy in talks to halt new Albania crisis.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky arrived in Albania on Thursday for last-ditch talks to get planned new elections back on track and stop the country sliding back into violence and lawlessness.

Vranitzky's fifth visit to Albania -- and his second in a week -- takes place amid hopes a new crisis can be averted after President Sali Berisha on Wednesday postponed a decree to call the vote, which most political parties had threatened to boycott in a dispute over a new electoral law.

The elections are seen as vital to make sure Albania does not plunge back into the unrest and violence which swept the country in February and March after the collapse of a string of high-yield-high-risk investment schemes cost thousands of people their life savings.
"We will see, we will have to wait and see," a tight-lipped Vranitzky said when asked if he was optimistic he could make a breakthrough.

The former Austrian chancellor, acting on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), was heading for a day of tough talking to persuade Albanian politicians to support the elections.
The vote is planned for June 29. To meet that deadline under Albanian law, Berisha has to issue the decree formally call the elections today -- 45 days before the proposed polling date.
Vranitzky was to hold meetings with Berisha, Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, Socialist Party Fatos Nano and the head of Berisha's Democratic Party, Tritan Shehu.
The envoy brokered a six-point political contract last week, under which the nine main parties agreed to pass a new electoral law and then call a vote for the end of June.

But trouble blew up as most of the parties of a nine-party interim Government of National Reconciliation said they would boycott the polls because Berisha's Democratic Party had pushed a law through parliament which gave it an advantage.
The smaller parties, led by the Socialists, want more seats allocated on a proportional basis while the Democratic Party favours more decided by majority vote.
They were also furious the law was presented by the Democrats rather than the government.
The Democratic Party insisted the law was in line with guidelines agreed last week with Vranitzky and the other parties.

A new crisis seemed certain after Berisha on Wednesday promised supporters he would dissolve parliament and call the elections despite the threatened boycott. But his office later said he had postponed the decree.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.

Another key point of the deal forged by Vranitzky was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees, formed mostly in the south of the country at the time of the rioting to bring back order as the state administration collapsed.

The agreement said they should disband 46 days before an election, but they have said they will break up only if the elections are guaranteed to be free and fair. A meeting of the committees is due on Friday.
